items.headline: XRISM observes stellar wind feeding a pulsar in BP Crucis
items.title: NASA-JAXA XRISM Mission Sees Pulsar Gathering Companion’s ‘Wind’
items.scifi_hook: Astronomers watch a giant star’s wind stream onto a compact pulsar, powering X‑ray flares.
items.eli5: A massive star blows gas that a nearby neutron star captures, creating bright X‑ray bursts.
items.why: It proves how matter transfer powers extreme X‑ray sources.
items.text: 5 min read NASA-JAXA XRISM Mission Sees Pulsar Gathering Companion’s ‘Wind’ Using data from the Japan-led XRISM (X-ray Imaging and Spectroscopy Mission) observatory, astronomers have directly observed a giant star’s outflow, called a stellar wind, being captured by its compact companion and providing the power source for strong X-ray flares. The research is part of NASA’s exploration of the extreme universe to better understand how the cosmos works. “We’ve never before seen clear indications of wind plasma falling onto a compact object,” said Roi Rahin, a researcher at UMBC (University of Maryland, Baltimore County) and NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland. “We can now test our understanding of these processes in much greater detail.” A paper describing the findings published Friday in the journal Science Advances. The target system is BP Crucis, a high-mass X-ray binary located about 13,000 light-years away in the southern constellation Crux. The primary star, known as Wray 977, is a blue hypergiant about 40 times the Sun’s mass and 60 times its size. It’s so big, hot, and luminous that ionized gas constantly streams away from it, a phenomenon astronomers call a stellar wind. This artist’s concept of the BP Crucis system follows the pulsar on a passage through the dense stream of plasma flowing from its companion, a blue hypergiant 40 times the Sun’s mass. During each four-day passage, the pulsar’s X-ray brightness flares as it pulls in some of the gas.

items.headline: COSI gamma‑ray telescope assembled for Milky Way studies
items.title: COSI Telescope Comes Together
items.scifi_hook: A new space‑borne gamma‑ray eye is being built to map matter‑antimatter fireworks across the galaxy.
items.eli5: Scientists are putting together a telescope that will detect high‑energy gamma rays from stars and explosions.
items.why: It will reveal energetic processes shaping our galaxy.
items.text: UC Berkeley/Alan Toth UC Berkeley engineers and managers watch as the COSI (Compton Spectrometer and Imager) detector assembly is slowly raised from a table in this July 8, 2026, image. The four pieces of silver material on the top of the detector box cover the flex circuits, which carry signals from the detectors to the readout electronics. COSI is a wide-field gamma-ray telescope that will study energetic phenomena in the Milky Way and beyond, including the creation and destruction of matter and antimatter and the final stages of the lives of stars. The mission is a collaboration between the University of California, Berkeley’s Space Sciences Laboratory; the University of California, San Diego; the Naval Research Laboratory; NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center; Northrop Grumman; Space Dynamics Laboratory; the Italian Space Agency; and a number of research institutions. Image credit: UC Berkeley/Alan Toth

items.headline: Copper supply risks cause first production decline since 2017
items.title: Copper mine supply risks first decline since 2017: Sprott
items.scifi_hook: Disruptions at major mines shave off 600,000 tonnes of copper, threatening power‑grid and AI growth.
items.eli5: Problems at big copper mines mean less copper will be produced this year, despite high prices.
items.why: Reduced copper supply could pressure prices for grids, AI data centers, and defense.
items.rationale: Supply constraints may lift copper prices
items.text: Global mined copper production could fall this year for the first time in nearly a decade even after prices hit records, as disruptions, declining grades and weak Chilean output expose how slowly miners can respond to higher prices, Sprott Asset Management says. Mine output fell 1.1% year over year in the first half of 2026, while disruptions at Freeport-McMoRan’s (NYSE: FCX) Grasberg mine in Indonesia and Ivanhoe Mines’ (TSX: IVN; US-OTC: IVPAF) Kamoa-Kakula complex in the Democratic Republic of Congo removed an estimated 600,000 tonnes of expected 2026 production, according to a new report this week by Sprott. That is equal to about 2.5% of annual global mine supply. “Higher prices improve project economics, but they cannot compress every stage of development or quickly replenish the discovery pipeline,” Jacob White, director of ETF product management at Sprott Asset Management, wrote in the report. Copper projects take about 17.5 years on average to move from discovery into production, he said. The constraint is colliding with rising demand from power grids, artificial intelligence data centres and defence, while U.S. tariff policy has shifted unusually large volumes of refined metal into American warehouses. Copper prices gained 47% in the 12 months through August, according to Toronto-based Sprott. It manages about C$77 billion ($55 billion) in assets. The spot copper price since mid-last year. items.headline: LHC rules out certain microscopic quantum black holes
items.title: Large Hadron Collider search rules out quantum black holes with certain properties
items.scifi_hook: Physicists extend LHC searches and find no evidence for tiny black holes that could link gravity to quantum forces.
items.eli5: Scientists looked for tiny black holes at the Large Hadron Collider and didn’t find them.
items.why: It narrows theories that try to unite gravity with quantum physics.
items.text: UC Santa Barbara physicists extended the search for microscopic black holes at the Large Hadron Collider, probing theories linking gravity to the universe’s basic forces.

items.headline: New polynomial error‑correcting colour codes boost quantum fault tolerance
items.title: Researchers Build Colour Codes with Polynomial Error Correction
items.scifi_hook: Researchers unveiled hyperbolic colour codes that protect quantum data with polynomial scaling, edging toward reliable quantum computers.
items.eli5: The new codes keep quantum bits safe longer by using math that grows protection faster than before.
items.why: Stronger error correction is essential for scaling practical quantum processors.
items.rationale: Improved codes could lift quantum hardware demand
items.text: Previous hyperbolic colour codes offered only logarithmic protection against computational errors. Now, constructions utilising arithmetic hyperbolic manifolds demonstrate polynomial scaling of both code distance *and* the number of logical qubits, a critical step towards dependable quantum processing in dimensions \(Dgeq 4\). This advance establishes a new family of error-correcting codes for exploring advanced fault tolerance.

items.headline: Simulations test icy moon ocean stability after cosmic impacts
items.title: Scientists simulate cosmic crashes to test whether icy moons gain or lose their ability to sustain life
items.scifi_hook: Scientists crash virtual comets into Saturn, Uranus and Neptune moons to see if their hidden oceans survive.
items.eli5: Computer models smash space rocks into icy moons to check if their underground seas stay intact for life.
items.why: Understanding ocean durability guides future missions searching for extraterrestrial life.
items.text: Many of the moons orbiting Saturn, Uranus and Neptune likely conceal oceans of liquid water beneath miles of icy shell. Because life as we know it needs water, these buried oceans rank among the most promising places to search for life beyond Earth.
